subject: community-medicine
title: Rabies Epidemiology: Exposure Categories and Wound Management

steps.title: Rabies virus pathogenesis and fatality
steps.tx: The bullet-shaped neurotropic Lyssavirus causing **rabies encephalitis** is transmitted in the saliva of rabid mammals through transdermal animal bites, scratches or mucosal contamination. Once inoculated into muscle tissue, the virus binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, entering unmyelinated peripheral nerve endings and ascending centripetally via retrograde axoplasmic transport into the spinal cord and brainstem, carrying a near hundred percent case fatality.
steps.say: Rabies is a bullet-shaped virus transmitted in animal saliva. It travels up peripheral nerves to the brain, producing fatal encephalitis once clinical symptoms appear.

steps.title: Animal vectors and Indian epidemiology
steps.tx: In India, free-roaming domestic and stray dogs account for approximately ninety-six to ninety-seven percent of all human rabies fatalities, maintaining intense **canine rabies** transmission in urban and rural environments. Cats, monkeys, wild jackals, foxes and wolves transmit the remainder of infections; in contrast, bites from rodents, squirrels, rabbits and domestic livestock exceptionally rarely transmit rabies, obviating post-exposure prophylaxis unless the biting animal demonstrated confirmed clinical madness.
steps.say: Stray dogs cause ninety-six percent of human rabies deaths in India. Wild jackals, foxes and monkeys also transmit the virus, whereas domestic rodents and squirrels do not spread rabies.

steps.title: Wound categorisation: WHO classification
steps.tx: Emergency triage follows the standard **WHO exposure categories** to determine appropriate prophylaxis following potential animal contact. Category I exposures involve touching, feeding animals or licks on intact healthy skin, carrying zero transmission risk and requiring no vaccination. Category II exposures comprise minor scratches, abrasions without bleeding, or nibbling of uncovered skin, demanding immediate wound washing and completion of a modern rabies vaccination course.
steps.say: Category one exposures involve touching animals on intact skin and require no shots. Category two covers minor scratches without bleeding, demanding immediate wound washing and vaccination.

steps.title: Category III bite management mandates
steps.tx: Severe exposures constitute a **category III bite**, defined by any transdermal bite or scratch that breaches the epidermis and draws blood, any licking of broken skin, mucous membrane contamination by saliva, or any unprovoked contact with wild carnivores and bats. These high-risk presentations demand an immediate three-step management protocol: thorough wound toilet, full active vaccination, and immediate infiltration of rabies immunoglobulin into and around all wound margins.
steps.say: Any animal bite that draws blood is a category three exposure. It demands immediate soap and water washing, a complete vaccine series, and rabies immunoglobulin injected around the wound.

steps.title: Immediate local wound washing
steps.tx: The single most effective intervention for preventing clinical rabies is immediate **wound toilet**, which washes away and inactivates inoculated viral particles before they enter local peripheral nerve endings. All bite wounds and scratches must be flushed vigorously under running tap water with soap or detergent for at least fifteen minutes, followed by povidone-iodine or alcohol; suturing is strictly avoided or delayed to prevent driving virus deeper into nerves.
steps.say: Washing the bite under running water with soap for fifteen minutes physically removes the virus. Never stitch an animal bite immediately, because needles push virus deeper into nerves.

steps.title: Post-exposure prophylaxis rationale
steps.tx: The life-saving success of modern **post-exposure prophylaxis** exploits the unusually long incubation period of rabies, which typically spans one to three months as the virus ascends peripheral nerves. Active vaccination stimulates host B lymphocytes to generate high titres of virus-neutralising antibodies, reaching protective thresholds of zero point five international units per millilitre before the slowly advancing pathogen can access the blood-brain barrier.
steps.say: Because rabies takes weeks to travel along nerves to the brain, vaccines administered promptly after a bite induce protective neutralising antibodies before the virus can reach the central nervous system.

steps.title: Intradermal rabies vaccination protocol
steps.tx: To overcome vaccine shortages and high costs, national policy adopted the **intradermal rabies vaccine** protocol across all government hospitals and primary health facilities. Modern cell culture vaccines or purified chick embryo cell vaccines are injected as zero point one millilitres intradermally over both deltoid muscles, cutting total required vaccine volume by sixty to eighty percent while generating equivalent or superior protective neutralising antibody titres.
steps.say: Injecting small zero point one millilitre doses intradermally into both deltoid muscles reduces vaccine costs by eighty percent while giving identical protection to intramuscular shots.

steps.title: National Rabies Control Programme
steps.tx: Under the One Health approach, the **National Rabies Control Programme** addresses human prophylaxis and animal reservoirs in a coordinated strategy. The human health component guarantees free modern tissue culture vaccines and rabies immunoglobulin in public emergency departments, while the animal health division implements mass dog anti-rabies vaccination drives and surgical animal birth control to achieve seventy percent herd immunity in street dog populations.
steps.say: The National Rabies Control Programme coordinates free human vaccines with mass street dog vaccination and sterilisation, aiming to stop transmission across species.

steps.title: Elimination goal and Rabies Free India
steps.tx: Aligned with the global target of **zero human rabies deaths** by 2030, the national action plan mobilises communities to eliminate dog-mediated rabies through digital bite registries, community awareness and rapid response teams. Health workers teach children never to provoke sleeping or feeding dogs, ensure mandatory bite reporting under national disease surveillance, and mandate post-exposure prophylaxis for every vulnerable exposed bite victim.
steps.say: India is working toward zero human rabies deaths by 2030. Achieving this goal requires digital reporting of all animal bites, school education, and guaranteed access to vaccines and immunoglobulin.
